title: Security — Secrets, API Key Rotation, Audit Logs, Guardrails

questions.question: What is the 2026 standard pattern for LLM service credentials?
options: Store keys in a Slack channel
Centralized vault pulled by an AI gateway at runtime via IAM role; rotate in vault and all apps pick up in minutes
Email the key to each engineer
Hardcode API keys in config files for speed
questions.explanation: The lesson describes the AI-gateway pattern as the 2026 standard: apps call a gateway, the gateway pulls credentials from a centralized vault at runtime via an IAM role, and rotating the key in the vault propagates to all apps within minutes, no redeploys needed.

questions.question: What rotation cadence does the lesson recommend for API keys, vault root tokens, and CI/CD credentials?
options: Within 90 days, automated where possible, logged and tracked when manual
Every 5 years
Only when leaked
Never
questions.explanation: The lesson states a rotation policy of 90 days or less for API keys, vault root tokens, and CI/CD credentials, automated where possible, with manual rotations logged and tracked.

questions.question: Why is consistent tokenization (Mesh approach) used for PII scrubbing?
options: It uses less memory than regex
It encrypts the prompt to the model
It is required by ISO 27001
Same source value maps to the same placeholder, so the LLM preserves code and relationship semantics across the prompt
questions.explanation: The lesson explains the Mesh approach maps the same source value to the same placeholder every time, so the LLM can still reason about relationships between entities in the prompt even though the actual PII values are masked.

questions.question: What egress posture does the lesson recommend for LLM service subnets?
options: Whitelist a small set of domains (api.openai.com, api.anthropic.com, vector DB, vault) and drop everything else, with an allowlist-only DNS resolver
Block all egress including providers
Allow DNS but block HTTP
Allow all outbound traffic
questions.explanation: The lesson recommends putting LLM services in a dedicated subnet that whitelists only the provider APIs, vector DB, and vault endpoints, drops everything else, and uses an allowlist-only DNS resolver to prevent DNS-tunneling exfiltration.

questions.question: What did the 2026 Vercel supply-chain incident teach about CI/CD credentials?
options: CI/CD credentials are prod-equivalent — store in vault, scope narrowly, rotate aggressively
CI/CD secrets cannot be stolen
CI/CD credentials are low-risk and can stay in env files
Vercel was unaffected
questions.explanation: The lesson cites compromised CI/CD credentials exfiltrating env vars across thousands of Vercel customer deployments as the lesson that CI/CD credentials are prod-equivalent and must be stored in vault, scoped narrowly, and rotated aggressively.

questions.question: Which audit log fields does the lesson recommend keeping for every LLM call?
options: Just the raw prompt
Only the response
Timestamp, user/tenant, prompt hash (not raw), model + version, token counts, cost, response hash, any guardrail trips
Only the cost
questions.explanation: The lesson's audit-log field list is exactly this: timestamp, user/tenant, prompt hash (not the raw prompt, for privacy), model and version, token counts, cost, response hash, and any guardrail trips.
